name: p3-0306-experiment-three-runs
title: The ten-minute experiment: the same job run three ways
spec: Three lanes for 8 jobs of burn(seed), each chaining 1,000,000 SHA-256 hashes. Lane 'sequential': one interpreter runs jobs 0 to 7 one after another. Lane '4 threads: ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4)': four threads share one GIL and take turns, so 'about as long as sequential, or a little longer' (orange). Lane '4 processes: ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=4)': four interpreters, each with its own GIL, 'clearly faster' on a machine with at least four free cores. Side note 'change burn to time.sleep(1) and rerun: now threads win because the GIL is released while a thread sleeps'. Strip 'timed() prints label and seconds with perf_counter; your timings depend on your hardware, so record your own'. Footnote 'a thread that computes for a long time is paused every 5 ms (sys.getswitchinterval()), an asyncio task is never paused that way and runs until an await'. Bottom bar: 'The GIL gives threads turns, processes get their own lock'.
alt: Eight CPU-bound hash jobs run sequentially, on four threads that take turns under one GIL and on four processes with separate GILs, with the sleep variant where threads win.
cap: Threads match the sequential time on CPU-bound work because of the GIL, processes are faster, and a sleep job reverses the result.

name: p3-0306-gil-releases
title: What the GIL releases, what it does not, and what it still lets break
spec: Three columns. Column 'Released during' (green or neutral): 'blocking I/O: socket calls, file reads, time.sleep, subprocess waits'; 'long native computations: NumPy, hashlib on large buffers, compression, regex in some cases, PyTorch ops, zlib, bz2'; result 'threads speed up I/O-bound and native-heavy code'. Column 'Held during': 'pure-Python CPU work'; result 'threads do not speed it up and can slow it down through contention and switching'. Column 'Not protected' (orange): 'x += 1 and a check-then-act on a dict can still race because individual bytecodes are atomic-ish but compound operations are not'; result 'the GIL does not remove the need for locks'. Why strip 'the GIL keeps reference counting safe and C extensions simpler to write'. Roadmap strip 'free-threaded CPython (PEP 703): optional build python3.13t, experimental from 3.13; subinterpreters (PEP 684 and PEP 734): own GIL each, concurrent.interpreters arrives in 3.14; other routes: processes, Cython, Numba, Rust through PyO3, NumPy, pandas, PyTorch'. Production strip 'gunicorn, uWSGI or uvicorn preforks one worker per core behind NGINX or Envoy; shared state moves to Redis, PostgreSQL, Celery or RabbitMQ'. Bottom bar: 'Threads help when the thread is waiting or the work is native, not when pure Python computes'.
alt: Three columns showing when the GIL is released, when it is held and what compound operations still race, with the free-threaded and subinterpreter roadmap and the prefork production pattern.
cap: The GIL is released for blocking I/O and native work, held for pure-Python computation, and never makes x += 1 safe.

name: p3-0306-pool-sizing
title: Size each pool by what limits it
spec: A three row table 'Model', 'What limits it', 'Pool size rule'. 'Threads doing I/O' / 'what the remote system can tolerate' / 'match the concurrency the remote tolerates, not the largest number you can start; 10 to 200 for blocking libraries (requests, paramiko, boto3)'. 'Processes doing CPU work' / 'cores' / 'os.cpu_count() or len(os.sched_getaffinity(0)), or the cgroup CPU limit in a container' (orange). 'asyncio' / 'target and sockets' / 'cap with a semaphore, for example Semaphore(100)'. Right panel 'Bounded concurrency first': 'unbounded fan-out overwhelms targets (thundering herd on a BMC network or an API, every client arrives at once), exhausts file descriptors and memory; set the limit before you write the loop'. Definition 'semaphore: a counter that lets at most that many tasks hold it at once'. Mixed strip 'async server plus blocking or CPU work: asyncio with to_thread or a process pool keeps the loop free'. Bottom bar: 'The limit is what keeps the fan-out safe'.
alt: A table giving the pool size rule for threads, processes and asyncio, with the reasons unbounded fan-out exhausts targets, descriptors and memory.
cap: Size thread pools by what the remote can tolerate, process pools by real cores, and asyncio by a semaphore, and set the limit before the loop.

name: p3-0306-thread-basics
title: Thread lifecycle and the rules that keep it stoppable
spec: A flow: 'Thread(target=worker, args=(t0, 1), name=worker-0, daemon=True)' to 'start()' to 'worker runs time.sleep(delay), which releases the GIL' to 'join(timeout=10) so a stuck thread shows up instead of freezing the script' to 'threading.active_count() and current_thread().name'. Left rule cards: 'daemon thread: killed abruptly at interpreter exit, no cleanup, only for chores you can afford to drop; non-daemon threads keep the process alive until they finish'. 'An exception inside a thread does not reach the main thread: it prints a traceback and ends; capture with futures or set threading.excepthook' (orange). 'No code can kill a thread from outside: use cooperative cancellation: a threading.Event to check, plus socket timeouts or queue.get(timeout=) on every blocking call'. 'threading.local() for state belonging to one thread; contextvars for context that follows tasks and threads'. Bottom bar: 'Design for cooperative stopping, because a thread cannot be killed'.
alt: A five-thread lifecycle from creation with daemon and name through start, sleep and join with timeout, with rules on daemon threads, lost exceptions and cooperative cancellation.
cap: Join with a timeout to detect stuck threads, capture thread errors with futures or excepthook, and stop threads with an Event rather than a kill.

name: p3-0306-lost-update
title: How counter += 1 loses an update, and what the lock changes
spec: Two thread lanes and a shared variable counter. Without lock (top): the steps of counter += 1 are 'load, add, store'. Thread A loads counter = 5; thread B loads counter = 5; A adds and stores 6; B adds and stores 6; final counter is 6 where two increments should give 7 (orange: 'one update lost'). With lock (bottom): 'with lock:' makes load, add and store one protected unit; A holds the lock, B waits; A stores 6; B then loads 6 and stores 7. Code strip 'lock = threading.Lock(); def incr(n): global counter; for _ in range(n): with lock: counter += 1'. Related bugs strip 'data race: loses updates or breaks an invariant; deadlock: two threads each hold a lock the other needs; livelock: keep reacting without progress; starvation: a thread never gets its turn; priority inversion: a low-priority task holds a lock a high-priority task needs'. Habits strip 'keep critical sections tiny and free of I/O; never call unknown callbacks while holding a lock; prefer queues and immutable messages; test with stress loops'. Bottom bar: 'Without the lock, the steps interleave'.
alt: Two threads interleaving the load, add and store steps of counter += 1 so one update is lost, beside the locked version that protects the three steps as one unit.
cap: Two threads can both load 5 and both store 6, and the lock turns load, add and store into one protected unit.

name: p3-0306-deadlock-fixes
title: Deadlock: two locks held in opposite order, and three ways out
spec: Left a wait cycle: 'thread 1 holds lock A and waits for lock B' and 'thread 2 holds lock B and waits for lock A'; both arrows form a loop labelled 'everything idle forever' (orange). Right three fixes: 'global lock order: always acquire A before B, so no cycle can form'; 'acquire with timeouts: give up, release, retry'; 'hold at most one lock'. Primitives table small: 'Lock: with lock:'; 'RLock: same thread may acquire repeatedly'; 'Event: set, clear, wait(timeout); shutdown signals'; 'Condition: wait_for(predicate) under a lock'; 'Semaphore or BoundedSemaphore: limit access to N resources (connection limits)'; 'Barrier: rendezvous N threads'; 'Timer: run after a delay'; 'queue.Queue, LifoQueue, PriorityQueue, SimpleQueue: maxsize bounds, task_done and join'. Diagnosis strip 'faulthandler.dump_traceback_later(60), py-spy dump, threading.enumerate(), sys._current_frames()'. Bottom bar: 'Ordering the locks removes the cycle'.
alt: Two threads each holding one lock and waiting for the other, with the three fixes of lock ordering, timeouts and a single lock, plus the table of threading primitives.
cap: A deadlock is a cycle of waits, and a global lock order, acquire timeouts or holding one lock break it.

name: p3-0306-sentinel-shutdown
title: Producer and consumers shut down with sentinels and task_done
spec: A flow. Left 'producer(items): for it in items: q.put(it)' blocks when the queue holds 100 items (maxsize=100) which is the backpressure. Middle 'queue.Queue(maxsize=100)'. Right N_CONSUMERS boxes 'consumer: while (item := q.get()) is not SENTINEL: try handle(item) finally q.task_done()'. After the last item the producer 'puts one SENTINEL per consumer' (orange) 'for _ in range(N_CONSUMERS): q.put(SENTINEL)' so each consumer sees exactly one and exits its loop. Note 'task_done() marks each item finished, so join() can tell when all the work is complete'. Rule strip 'SENTINEL = object(): nothing else can equal it'. Contrast strip 'asyncio version: bounded Queue(maxsize), await q.put() waits while full, q.join() waits until all queued items are processed'. Bottom bar: 'One sentinel per consumer tells each of them that no work is left'.
alt: A producer filling a queue bounded at 100, consumers calling task_done in a finally block and one sentinel per consumer ending each loop, with the asyncio equivalent.
cap: Put one sentinel for each consumer after the last item, and let task_done and join tell you when the work is finished.

name: p3-0306-map-vs-as-completed
title: pool.map versus as_completed with 20 hosts and a slow second host
spec: Two timelines of 20 hosts where host 2 is slow. Top 'pool.map(fn, hosts, timeout=..)': results come out in input order; hosts 3 to 20 sit finished but unreported until host 2 returns, so a progress display appears to freeze even though workers are busy; raises the first exception when that item is reached. Bottom (orange) 'as_completed over futs = {pool.submit(check, h): h for h in hosts}': each future is yielded as soon as it finishes; 'one slow host does not hold up the report'; 'h = futs[fut]' ties each exception to the host that caused it; 'fut.result() re-raises the worker's exception here' inside try/except Exception that records errors[h] = repr(exc); overall deadline 'as_completed(futs, timeout=120)'. Future methods strip 'result(timeout), exception(), add_done_callback(), done(), cancel() works only if the task has not started'. Shutdown strip 'leaving the with block waits for pending work (shutdown(wait=True)); on exception shutdown(wait=False, cancel_futures=True) from 3.9 drops queued tasks; executors do not interrupt running tasks when a timeout expires, so set timeouts on the I/O inside each task'. Output example '50 workers, thread_name_prefix=probe, print(len(results), ok; len(errors), failed)'. Bottom bar: 'Order of input is not order of completion'.
alt: Two timelines for 20 hosts with a slow second host, where pool.map holds back hosts 3 to 20 while as_completed reports each result as it finishes and maps errors back to hosts.
cap: pool.map yields in input order so one slow host freezes progress, while as_completed with a future-to-host dictionary reports live and tags each error.

name: p3-0306-client-thread-safety
title: Which objects you may share between threads
spec: A table 'Object', 'Safe to share?', 'Note'. 'queue.Queue' / 'yes' / '-'. 'logging' / 'yes' / '-'. 'single list.append and pop; single dict operations' / 'yes' / 'compound operations are not safe'. 'boto3 low-level client' / 'documented thread-safe' / 'boto3 sessions and resources are not'. 'requests.Session' / 'mostly, for simple use' / 'documentation makes no strong guarantee'. 'paramiko SSHClient' / 'no' / 'open one connection per worker' (orange). 'sqlite3 connection' / 'refuses another thread by default' / '-'. 'Database drivers' / 'check the DB-API threadsafety attribute of the driver module' / 'tells you whether threads may share the module, a connection or neither'. Footer 'when in doubt create one client per thread with threading.local()'. Bottom bar: 'Never assume a client object is safe to share'.
alt: A table of objects and whether threads may share them, including queue, logging, boto3 client versus session, requests Session, paramiko SSHClient and sqlite3, with the threading.local fallback.
cap: Queues and logging are safe to share, SSH clients are not, and one client per thread with threading.local is the fallback.

name: p3-0306-start-methods
title: fork, spawn and forkserver: how a worker process is born
spec: Three columns. Column 'fork': 'copies the parent quickly; child shares memory pages, copy-on-write means a page is copied only when one side writes it; unsafe with threads, locks held at fork time, CUDA contexts and open sockets; default on Linux up to Python 3.13'. Column 'spawn' : 'starts a fresh interpreter that imports your module; safe but slower; needs picklable arguments and the if __name__ == "__main__" guard; default on macOS and Windows'. Column 'forkserver': 'a clean server process forks the workers; became the default on Linux and other POSIX systems except macOS in Python 3.14'. Warning bar (orange) 'Never use fork after initialising CUDA: that is why PyTorch DataLoader workers and distributed launchers use spawn or forkserver'; also avoid forking with running threads or gRPC or OpenMP state. Select strip 'multiprocessing.set_start_method("spawn") or mp_context=multiprocessing.get_context("forkserver")'. Cost strip 'each process takes tens of milliseconds to start plus import time; use chunking, long-lived workers and coarse tasks'. Bottom bar: 'Fork fast, spawn safe'.
alt: Three columns comparing fork, spawn and forkserver on how they start workers, which are safe with threads and CUDA and which are the defaults on Linux, macOS and Windows.
cap: fork is fast but unsafe with threads and CUDA, spawn is safe but needs picklable arguments, and forkserver is the Linux default from Python 3.14.

name: p3-0306-process-boundary
title: What crosses a process boundary: pickle, shared memory and failure
spec: A left to right diagram of parent and worker with a pickle channel between. Arrows 'arguments pickled' and 'results pickled'. Cannot be pickled (orange): 'lambdas, nested functions, open files, sockets, locks'; error 'Can't pickle local object'; fix 'top-level functions and plain data'. Large objects 'are copied, which is slow: pass file paths or indices instead'. Sharing tools column: 'multiprocessing.Queue, Pipe, Manager', 'Value and Array (ctypes, with locks)', 'multiprocessing.shared_memory.SharedMemory: zero-copy buffers, basis for NumPy arrays shared across processes', 'numpy.memmap memory-mapped files', 'under fork, read-only data is shared copy-on-write; reference-count writes can trigger page copies; gc.freeze() helps'. Pool features strip 'Pool: map, imap_unordered, apply_async, starmap; maxtasksperchild recycles leaky workers; initializer sets per-worker state such as opening a model or a database connection; chunksize=16 batches IPC for many small tasks'. Failure strip 'an exception in a worker re-raises in the parent with its traceback text; if the kernel's out-of-memory killer stops a worker you get BrokenProcessPool, which you must handle and recover from'. Bottom bar: 'Send paths and indices, not big objects'.
alt: A parent and worker connected by a pickle channel, listing what cannot be pickled, how to share large data with SharedMemory and memmap and how worker failures and BrokenProcessPool surface.
cap: Arguments and results are pickled, so send paths instead of large objects, and use SharedMemory for zero-copy sharing.

name: p3-0306-container-cpus
title: In a container, count the cores you really get
spec: A comparison of two numbers on a container started with --cpus=2. Left 'os.cpu_count()' reports the host's CPUs, for example the whole machine (orange: wrong number to size a pool by). Right 'len(os.sched_getaffinity(0))' or read the cgroup cpu.max file. Consequence chain: 'pool sized by the host count' to 'oversubscribed container' to 'the kernel throttles it' to 'throttling shows up in cpu.stat' to 'slow runs'. Related trap 'nested parallelism: a NumPy BLAS threads times a process pool oversubscribes the cores; set OMP_NUM_THREADS=1'. Orphan strip 'under fork children inherit signal handlers: handle SIGTERM in the parent and call pool.terminate(); if the parent is killed with SIGKILL, workers can be orphaned: use prctl(PR_SET_PDEATHSIG) or a supervisor such as systemd or Kubernetes; use daemon=True with care'. Bottom bar: 'Size pools to the cores your container really gets, and keep the tasks coarse'.
alt: A container with a two CPU limit where os.cpu_count reports the host while sched_getaffinity or cpu.max gives the real count, with the throttling chain and the nested BLAS parallelism warning.
cap: os.cpu_count reports host CPUs, so use sched_getaffinity or the cgroup limit, and watch throttling in cpu.stat.

name: p3-0306-gpu-one-process
title: One process per GPU, with threads only for I/O
spec: A node with GPU ranks. Each GPU box maps to one process (a rank) launched by 'torchrun, accelerate, DeepSpeed, mpirun or Slurm srun'. Between ranks the label 'NCCL handles communication (Part 14)'. Inside each rank two kinds of workers: 'DataLoader(num_workers=N) worker processes decode and augment data; tune num_workers, prefetch_factor, pin_memory, persistent_workers' and 'threads inside a rank are for I/O such as prefetching, not for compute' (orange). Warning strip 'avoid forking after CUDA is initialised; watch for memory duplication'. Bottom bar: 'Keep one process per GPU, and let threads handle only the I/O'.
alt: GPU ranks each run as one process started by a launcher, with DataLoader worker processes for decoding and threads inside a rank used only for I/O, linked by NCCL.
cap: Run one process per GPU, use DataLoader workers for decoding, and keep threads inside a rank for I/O only.

name: p3-0306-gather-vs-taskgroup
title: gather versus TaskGroup when one task fails
spec: Two lanes with three tasks, the second failing. Lane 'gather(*aws, return_exceptions=False)': first exception propagates, the other tasks keep running; with 'return_exceptions=True' exceptions are collected in the results list alongside values. Lane 'async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg: tg.create_task(poll(n, results))' (orange, structured concurrency, 3.11): tasks started in the group are awaited on exit; if one fails the others are cancelled and an ExceptionGroup is raised; 'except* TimeoutError as eg: log.error(timeouts: ..., [str(e) for e in eg.exceptions])' then 'return results'. Strip 'asyncio.create_task(coro) schedules concurrently; keep a reference because the loop holds only weak references and a dropped task can be garbage collected mid-flight'. Strip 'await suspends the caller until the awaited coroutine, future or task completes; only inside async def; calling an async def returns a coroutine object that has not run yet'. Bottom bar: 'A TaskGroup leaves no orphan task behind'.
alt: gather with return_exceptions False or True compared with a TaskGroup where a failure cancels the siblings and raises an ExceptionGroup handled by except star.
cap: gather lets other tasks keep running after a failure, while TaskGroup cancels the siblings and raises an ExceptionGroup.

name: p3-0306-cancel-timeout
title: Cancellation and timeouts: what happens at the await
spec: A sequence for task.cancel(). Step 1 'task.cancel() requested'. Step 2 'asyncio.CancelledError is raised at the task's current await'. Step 3 'cleanup in a finally block'. Step 4 'say it again: re-raise CancelledError, never swallow it' (orange). Branch 'swallowed with a bare except: cannot cancel or shut down'. Side tool 'asyncio.shield() protects critical sections'. Timeout panel 'await asyncio.wait_for(coro, timeout) or async with asyncio.timeout(10): (3.11)'; 'every network await needs a timeout: without one a half-open connection waits forever and you get a silent hang'; 'timeouts and TaskGroup both rely on cancellation'. Primitive panel 'asyncio Lock, Semaphore, Event, Condition, Queue are async versions of the thread primitives; not thread-safe across threads; bounded Queue: await q.put() waits while full; Semaphore(100) throttles active HTTP requests'. Bottom bar: 'Cancellation is an exception delivered at an await'.
alt: The steps of task.cancel from CancelledError at the current await to finally cleanup and re-raise, with the swallowing bug, shield, wait_for and timeout and the async primitives.
cap: cancel raises CancelledError at the current await, so clean up in finally and re-raise, and put a timeout on every network await.

name: p3-0306-async-protocol-map
title: Async iteration, generators and comprehensions: what runs when
spec: A table of constructs. 'async for over an async iterable' / '__aiter__ returns an asynchronous iterator whose async def __anext__ raises StopAsyncIteration when it runs out'. 'async with' / 'enters and exits through __aenter__ and __aexit__, or contextlib.asynccontextmanager builds the pair'. 'async generator' / 'async def with yield; example: a probe starts one coroutine per host, loops over asyncio.as_completed, awaits each finished one and yields its result'. 'PEP 530 comprehensions' / '[x ** 2 async for x in AsyncRange(1, 5)]', '{name: found async for name, found in multi_probe(names)}', '{name for name in names if (await probe(name)).found}'. Warning (orange) 'async for awaits each item in turn as the iterator yields it; to run a batch concurrently use await asyncio.gather(*coros) or asyncio.TaskGroup'. Blocking bridge strip 'await asyncio.to_thread(save, data, path) for blocking file writes; writer.write(data); await writer.drain(); asyncio.create_subprocess_exec(*cmd, stdout=PIPE) then await proc.communicate() reads both streams and avoids pipe deadlocks'. Bottom bar: 'Each await is a place where the loop can switch tasks'.
alt: A table of async for, async with, async generators and PEP 530 comprehensions with the rule that async for is sequential, plus to_thread, drain and create_subprocess_exec bridges.
cap: async for waits for each item in turn, so use gather or TaskGroup for concurrency and to_thread for blocking calls.

name: p3-0306-blocking-loop-fix
title: One blocking call freezes every task, and how to route work off the loop
spec: Top lane: a single event loop thread with tasks A, B, C. Task B calls 'time.sleep, requests.get, subprocess.run or heavy CPU' (orange): 'a task is never paused except at an await, so all other tasks stall; timeouts fire everywhere'. Bottom routing table: 'blocking function' to 'await asyncio.to_thread(blocking_fn, args) (3.9) or loop.run_in_executor(executor, fn, *args)'; 'CPU-bound function' to 'run_in_executor with a ProcessPoolExecutor'; 'sync libraries requests, paramiko, boto3' to 'wrap with to_thread'; 'async libraries: aiohttp, httpx, asyncssh, aiofiles (uses threads under the hood), asyncpg, redis.asyncio, aiokafka, kubernetes_asyncio, aioboto3, aiobotocore, grpc.aio'. Debug strip 'asyncio.run(main(), debug=True) or PYTHONASYNCIODEBUG=1 logs callbacks longer than 100 ms (loop.slow_callback_duration), coroutines never awaited and tasks destroyed while pending; asyncio.all_tasks() and task.print_stack() show where tasks are stuck; py-spy dump --pid when the loop itself is blocked'. Side note 'uvloop: faster drop-in loop on Linux and macOS'. Bottom bar: 'Keep the loop free'.
alt: An event loop where one task makes a blocking call and stalls the others, with the routing of blocking and CPU-bound work to to_thread or executors and the debug-mode tools.
cap: A blocking call in a coroutine stalls every task, so route it to to_thread or a process pool and use debug mode to find the slow callbacks.

name: p3-0306-pool-template-flow
title: The worker-pool template: who waits for whom, and how shutdown works
spec: A flow of run_pool(items, handler, concurrency=50, queue_size=500). Left producer 'for it in items: await q.put(it)' into 'asyncio.Queue(maxsize=queue_size) bounded: producer awaits when workers lag'. Middle 50 workers 'worker(name, q, results, handler): item = await q.get(); results.append(await asyncio.wait_for(handler(item), timeout=30)); except CancelledError: raise; except Exception: log.warning and results.append(exc); finally q.task_done()'. Signal box (orange) 'loop.add_signal_handler(SIGINT and SIGTERM, stop.set); the producer checks stop.is_set() and breaks'. Shutdown steps 'await q.join() waits until all queued items are processed' then 'finally: for w in workers: w.cancel()' then 'await asyncio.gather(*workers, return_exceptions=True)' then 'return results'. Properties strip 'bounded memory, bounded concurrency, per-item timeouts, error isolation, clean cancellation on signals; tune concurrency and queue_size to what your targets can take'. Bottom bar: 'A fleet loop you can trust'.
alt: A bounded asyncio queue feeding fifty workers with per-item timeouts and error isolation, a stop event set by signal handlers, then join, cancel and gather to shut down cleanly.
cap: The template bounds memory and concurrency, isolates errors per item and cancels workers cleanly after join or a signal.

name: p3-0306-retry-arithmetic
title: The retry helper: delay range per attempt with real numbers
spec: A table for retry(fn, attempts=5, base=0.5, cap=20.0) with full jitter delay = random.uniform(0, min(cap, base * 2 ** i)). Rows: 'attempt i=0: ceiling min(20, 0.5 * 1) = 0.5 s, delay between 0 and 0.5'; 'i=1: ceiling 1.0 s'; 'i=2: ceiling 2.0 s'; 'i=3: ceiling 4.0 s'; 'i=4: the last attempt, no sleep, the error is re-raised' (orange). Rules panel 'retry only idempotent operations (safe to repeat: twice leaves the same result as once) and transient errors: timeouts, connection resets, 429 or 503; cap the total time; honour Retry-After; log each attempt'. Libraries strip 'tenacity, backoff, urllib3.util.Retry with requests.adapters.HTTPAdapter'. Bottom bar: 'Full jitter keeps many clients from retrying together'.
alt: A table of the retry helper with base 0.5 and cap 20 showing each attempt's random delay ceiling of 0.5, 1, 2 and 4 seconds and the final re-raise, with the retry rules.
cap: Each failed attempt waits a random time up to the smaller of the cap and base times two to the attempt, and the last attempt re-raises.

name: p3-0306-protect-targets
title: Protecting targets and yourself: limits, breaker, and the final report
spec: Two panels. Panel 'Protect the targets': 'token bucket (aiolimiter, or an asyncio semaphore plus a sleep) limits the rate'; 'per-host concurrency limits: one semaphore per host, rack or BMC network'; 'circuit breaker stops calling a failing dependency for a cool-down so it can recover'; 'honour Retry-After; adaptive concurrency such as AIMD, the approach TCP uses'; 'for BMC and Redfish fleets limit concurrency per rack so management switches are not overwhelmed' (orange). Panel 'Aggregating results': 'return Result(host, ok, value or error, duration) for each item'; 'summarise: success and failure counts, slowest items, error classes'; 'exit non-zero if a critical failure occurred'; 'keep raw errors for diagnosis'; 'do not let one exception abort everything unless you mean it to: return_exceptions=True or catch inside the worker'. Bottom bar: 'A fleet run ends with a report, not a crash'.
alt: Two panels listing target protections such as token buckets, per-rack limits and circuit breakers, and the Result record fields and summary of an aggregated fleet report.
cap: Limit rate and concurrency per target, break the circuit on failure, and finish every fleet run with a per-item Result summary.

name: p3-0306-pipeline-and-schedule
title: Paged pipelines and drift-free periodic loops
spec: Two panels. Panel 'Streaming and pagination': producer 'async for page in client.list_pages(): await q.put(page)' into bounded queue into several consumers 'process pages in parallel under bounded concurrency'; 'memory stays flat because the queue bound limits how many pages wait at once'. Panel 'Periodic loop': 'while not stop.is_set(): await run_once(); await asyncio.wait_for(stop.wait(), timeout=interval)'; 'the wait is interruptible, so a stop signal ends the loop without waiting out the full interval' (orange); 'use time.monotonic() for intervals that do not drift; compute the next deadline instead of sleeping a fixed amount so drift does not build up'; 'cron-style schedules: systemd timers, Kubernetes CronJobs or APScheduler'. Bottom bar: 'Wait on the stop event, not on a bare sleep'.
alt: A page producer feeding a bounded queue and parallel consumers, beside a periodic loop that waits on a stop event with a timeout and computes the next deadline from monotonic time.
cap: A bounded queue keeps paged pipelines flat in memory, and waiting on a stop event with a timeout makes the periodic loop interruptible.

name: p3-0306-combine-models
title: Bridges between the three models
spec: A diagram with three boxes 'asyncio loop', 'thread pool' and 'process pool' and labelled arrows. 'loop to process pool: await loop.run_in_executor(process_pool, cpu_fn, data)'. 'loop to thread: await asyncio.to_thread(...)'. 'thread to loop: asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe(coro, loop) and loop.call_soon_threadsafe'. Side panel 'Multiprocess web servers: gunicorn or uvicorn workers each have their own event loop, so they scale across cores; share state through external stores such as Redis, not through memory'. Side panel 'FastAPI BackgroundTasks: short fire-and-forget work; for durable work use real queues (chapter 3.7)'. Distributed strip 'beyond one machine: Slurm job arrays and srun, Kubernetes Jobs with completions, parallelism and indexed jobs, Ray remote functions and actors, Dask, Celery and RQ workers; at that scale idempotency, checkpointing and at-least-once semantics (a task may run more than once but must never be silently lost) matter more than the in-process model' (orange). Bottom bar: 'Design for idempotency, checkpointing and at-least-once first, then choose the framework'.
alt: Three boxes for the asyncio loop, thread pool and process pool joined by run_in_executor, to_thread and run_coroutine_threadsafe, with multiprocess servers and distributed options.
cap: Models connect through run_in_executor, to_thread and run_coroutine_threadsafe, and distributed work needs idempotency, checkpoints and at-least-once first.

name: p3-0306-symptom-ladder
title: From symptom to likely cause, with the first tool to use
spec: A three column table, symptom to cause to remedy. 'Tasks stall, timeouts everywhere, slow callback warnings' / 'blocking the event loop' / 'async APIs or to_thread'. 'Work never happens; was never awaited warning' / 'un-awaited coroutine' / 'await or create_task'. 'Task exception was never retrieved' / 'dropped task reference' / 'keep references, await or add done callbacks'. 'Cannot cancel or shut down' / 'swallowed CancelledError' / 're-raise it, no bare except'. 'Hangs after network blips' / 'missing timeouts' / 'wait_for or timeout on every await; client timeout='. 'OOM, too many open files, target overload' / 'unbounded fan-out' / 'semaphores, bounded queues, islice feeding'. 'Rare wrong results' / 'thread-unsafe shared state' / 'locks, queues, thread-local, immutable data'. 'Everything idle forever' / 'deadlock' / 'lock ordering, timeouts; faulthandler.dump_traceback_later(60); py-spy dump'. 'Hangs in children, CUDA errors' / 'fork with threads, CUDA or locks' / 'spawn or forkserver'. 'Can't pickle local object' / 'pickle errors' / 'top-level functions'. 'Memory growth in pools' / 'worker leaks' / 'maxtasksperchild, tracemalloc'. 'Defunct processes, leftover workers' / 'zombies or orphans' / 'wait(), context managers, process groups, supervisors'. 'CPU throttling, slow runs' / 'oversubscription' / 'match cgroup limits, OMP_NUM_THREADS=1'. 'Target collapse' / 'thundering herd or retry storm' / 'jittered backoff, limits, circuit breakers'. 'Silent partial results' / 'lost exceptions in threads' / 'futures, threading.excepthook'. 'ValueError: signal only works in main thread' / 'signal in a non-main thread' / 'install handlers in the main thread or loop.add_signal_handler'. 'RuntimeError' / 'asyncio.run() inside a running loop (Jupyter)' / 'await instead; nest_asyncio only for notebooks'. Highlight in orange the first two habits 'a timeout on every wait, a bound on every queue and pool'. Bottom bar: 'Start from the symptom you see'.
alt: A table mapping seventeen concurrency symptoms to their likely cause and remedy, from stalled tasks and hangs to OOM, deadlocks, fork problems and RuntimeError in notebooks.
cap: Most symptoms trace back to a missing timeout, an unbounded queue or pool, or a blocking call on the loop.

name: p3-0306-diagnosis-tools
title: Which diagnosis tool answers which question
spec: A table 'Question' to 'Tool'. 'Where is every thread stuck right now?' / 'faulthandler.enable(), faulthandler.dump_traceback_later(timeout, repeat=True), kill -SIGUSR1 with faulthandler.register'. 'Look at a running process without changing its code' / 'py-spy dump, py-spy top, py-spy record'. 'What threads and tasks exist?' / 'threading.enumerate(), sys._current_frames(), asyncio.all_tasks(), psutil.Process().num_threads()'. 'Sockets and descriptors' / 'ss -s, lsof -p'. 'System calls and CPU' / 'strace -f -p, perf'. 'Where memory grows' / 'tracemalloc'. 'Health metrics to track' / 'in-flight tasks, queue depth, latency percentiles' (orange). Chain strip 'symptom, then faulthandler dump or py-spy dump, then the cause in the pitfall table'. Bottom bar: 'Sample the live process before you guess'.
alt: A table pairing diagnosis questions with faulthandler, py-spy, thread and task listings, ss and lsof, strace and perf, tracemalloc and the metrics worth tracking.
cap: faulthandler and py-spy show where a live process is stuck, and in-flight tasks, queue depth and latency percentiles are the metrics to track.

name: p3-0306-mistake-groups
title: Common mistakes grouped by theme
spec: Seven groups as a table 'Theme', 'Mistake', 'Fix'. 'Wrong tool' / 'threads for CPU-bound pure Python; asyncio with blocking libraries never offloaded; treating async as faster by default (for a handful of requests the overhead is not worth it)' / 'processes for CPU, to_thread for blocking calls'. 'Unbounded work' / 'no semaphore, queue or pool limit; unbounded queues; millions of futures' / 'bound everything'. 'Quiet error handling' / 'missing timeouts; swallowed CancelledError; fire-and-forget tasks without references; forgetting to collect worker exceptions; aborting a fleet operation on the first failure' / 'timeouts, references, aggregated results'. 'Shared state' / 'sharing mutable state across threads or processes; assuming the GIL makes code thread-safe' / 'pass messages'. 'Process setup' / 'forking after threads or CUDA; missing if __name__ == "__main__" with spawn; unpicklable objects' / 'spawn or forkserver, top-level functions'. 'Retries' / 'retrying non-idempotent operations; no jitter and caps' (orange) / 'idempotent only, full jitter, caps'. 'Pool sizing' / 'sizing by cpu_count() inside containers; a process pool over BLAS threads' / 'cgroup-aware count'. Bottom bar: 'Before you ship: every pool and queue has a limit, and every await has a timeout'.
alt: A grouped table of concurrency mistakes in tool choice, unbounded work, error handling, shared state, process setup, retries and pool sizing, each with its fix.
cap: Check that every pool and queue has a limit and every await has a timeout before shipping.
